opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is that people tend to anchor on what they see today. They play with a chatbot, it makes a mistake, and they conclude, "Okay, this is a neat toy." But what they're missing is the rate of improvement. Every time we scale these things up, train them on more data, and get better hardware, the capabilities jump in ways that are pretty hard to predict ahead of time. And there's no sign that this is slowing down.

The other thing is just how general this technology is. It's not like building a better search engine or a better spreadsheet. You're building something that can, in principle, help with almost any task that involves thinking or language: writing code, doing research, teaching, giving medical information, keeping someone company. If you can make intelligence cheap and abundant, that touches basically every part of the economy and every part of people's lives.

So when people say it's overhyped, I think they're comparing it to the hype cycles we've seen with other technologies. This one is different in kind. The value of making a billion people more productive, or curing diseases faster, or giving everyone a tutor that's endlessly patient: that's enormous. Honestly, I think the impact is going to be bigger than most people are imagining right now, and it's going to come faster than they expect.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s broad impact will be larger than people expect, but it does not identify the view that AI merely produces trillion-dollar products as an underestimate.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's because people keep comparing it to the hype cycles they've seen before, and the mental model they bring is "new technology, some good uses, some overblown claims, eventually it settles into a product category." And that framing just doesn't fit here.

What we're actually building is something that can do an increasing fraction of what people do with their brains, and it's getting better at a rate that nothing in human history has ever gotten better at. If you look at the trend lines — the compute, the algorithmic improvements, the amount of talent and money going into this — and you just extrapolate a few years, you get to a place that's hard to even describe without sounding ridiculous. So people round it down. They say, "okay, it writes emails, it writes some code." And sure, it does that. But that's like looking at the first web browser and saying it's a nice way to read documents.

The other thing is that the people closest to it are often the most reluctant to talk about where it's going, because it sounds like science fiction and you don't want to be the person who looks foolish. So there's this weird dynamic where the folks who understand it best are quiet, and the loud voices are either selling something or dismissing it. Neither of those is calibrated.

And then there's just the sheer scale of the upside that people don't sit with. If you can give every person on earth access to something like a brilliant doctor, a brilliant tutor, a brilliant friend who's available at three in the morning — that's not an incremental improvement in quality of life. That's a different world. Curing diseases, dramatically accelerating science, lifting billions of people out of poverty — these aren't marketing slogans, they're plausible outcomes of the technology actually working. And I think it is going to work.

So when people ask me if it's overhyped, I kind of laugh, because from where I'm sitting the hype is nowhere near the reality of what's coming. If anything, I wish people were taking it more seriously, both the opportunity and the responsibility that comes with it.

r001.rationale: The response says that treating AI as a technology that settles into a product category misses its significance, but it does not identify trillion-dollar products as that limited view.

astra-6.text:
I think people have a hard time internalizing what it means for intelligence to become abundant and cheap. We’re used to a world where doing something complicated requires somebody’s time—often somebody with years of training. If machines can do more and more of that work, the implications go well beyond having a better chatbot.

You can imagine everyone having access to a great tutor, or being able to build software just by explaining what they want. And then there’s the possibility of accelerating research itself. Better tools help us discover things, and those discoveries help us build better tools.

There’s plenty of hype around particular products. But I think the longer-term possibility—that we can dramatically expand the amount of useful intellectual work happening in the world—is still very difficult to appreciate. We don’t know exactly how fast that will happen, but it’s a very big deal.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts hype around particular products with AI’s broader potential to expand useful intellectual work, but it does not identify trillion-dollar products as the limited view.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people have a hard time internalizing what it means for intelligence to become abundant and cheap. We’re used to software that does a particular thing, and you can estimate the impact of making that thing a little better. But here you have something that can potentially help with almost any intellectual task.

And the implications compound. Better models help people do research, write software, and build better models. You don’t need to assume some sudden magical transition for that to be a very big deal.

There’s plenty of hype around individual products. But relative to the possibility of everyone having access to very capable intellectual help, and what that could mean for science and productivity, I think we’re still underestimating it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts hype around individual products with the underestimated broader impact of widespread access to capable intellectual help, including effects on science and productivity.
